Qualcomm is reportedly planning to lay off some of its employees globally. According to a Reuters report, the job cuts are part of a "performance-focused reduction" following the annual employee reviews. Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon has sent a memo to the staff, informing them of ‌notifications beginning in November. As stated in the report, CEO Amon said in the memo that the job cuts are part of an effort to build "a stronger performance culture" and address situations where the company "has consistently fallen short of expectations".Qualcomm has about 52,000 employees globally as of September last year. The memo, however, did not reveal the number of employees that will be affected by the layoffs.Amon said the job cuts would be based on the company’s business priorities, organisational needs, and the skills and expertise required."As we have expanded the business, so have the competencies ⁠and skills ​we require," Critiano Amon wrote. "We must have the right ​people in the right roles so they can perform at their best and the company can continue ​to succeed."
Qualcomm is one of the world's biggest smartphone chipmakers.
It has been hit this year by a slump in consumer electronics sales as rising memory prices impacted demand in key markets. The company’s shares have risen just 1.5% in 2026, compared with gains of more than ​12% for the benchmark S&P 500 and nearly 60% for the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index.Qualcomm released its latest earnings report earlier this year in July. The company then forecasted quarterly profit below estimates and said revenue from Apple products would decline faster than expected. However, it then signalled that growth in data-center and ​other non-handset businesses would ​more than offset ⁠the lost revenue by fiscal 2027. The company expects most of its chip sales to come from industries outside smartphones in fiscal 2027 as it expands into the fast-growing AI data centre market.

Qualcomm rejects Snapdragon overheating claims amid reports of Samsung testing problems, raising questions about the Galaxy S27 Ultra’s processor.
Qualcomm has rejected overheating allegations involving its Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 processor as questions persist about Samsung's Galaxy S27 Ultra chip choice. Image: Qualcomm Technologies, Inc.

Qualcomm is rejecting overheating allegations involving its most powerful new smartphone processor, as questions grow over whether Samsung will use the chip in its Galaxy S27 Ultra.
On October 17, Qualcomm rejected reports of thermal problems with the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6. The response followed South Korean reporting that Samsung had encountered performance slowdowns while testing the processor and was considering its Exynos 2700 chip as an alternative.
Samsung has not confirmed the alleged findings or announced a processor change. The dispute leaves questions about how Qualcomm’s new flagship chip will perform under sustained workloads in finished phones.
Qualcomm disputes Samsung testing allegations
The allegations originated in an October 16 Seoul Economic Daily report, which cited industry sources claiming Samsung’s internal tests found excessive temperatures and repeated performance slowdowns during demanding workloads.
Samsung reportedly requested improvements from Qualcomm and was weighing the Exynos 2700 if the Snapdragon processor failed to meet its requirements. Subsequent reporting indicated discussions could continue through the end of October.
Qualcomm rejected the allegations in a statement to 9to5Google, describing reports of thermal problems involving the Extreme chip as “inaccurate.”
Chief Marketing Officer Don McGuire separately wrote on X that there were “no systemic thermal issues” with the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6. He added that manufacturers routinely adjust performance and power consumption during device development.
McGuire did not explicitly identify the Extreme variant in his remarks, an ambiguity highlighted by Android Authority on October 19. Qualcomm’s separate statement addressed that processor directly, but neither company has publicly released data establishing whether the alleged problems occurred.
Qualcomm’s official specifications list a 2-nanometer manufacturing process and CPU speeds reaching 5GHz. Those figures describe the processor’s capabilities, not how consistently finished devices can maintain peak performance.
Qualcomm also introduced a standard Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6, with its features detailed in a separate platform overview. Samsung has not announced plans to replace Snapdragon in its Galaxy S27 Ultra.
Thermal throttling reduces processor speeds as temperatures rise. Although normal in modern chips, excessive throttling can disrupt demanding workloads, including gaming, prolonged video recording and on-device AI processing.
Peak benchmark scores cannot establish sustained performance on their own. Cooling hardware, battery capacity and software tuning also influence how individual smartphones manage heat.
Motorola’s upcoming Signature 27 flagship will feature the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 and an ArcticMesh cooling system designed to sustain performance under load. Whether that design delivers consistent results will require independent testing.
Organizations evaluating Snapdragon-powered phones should compare performance, battery behavior and temperatures during repeated workloads rather than relying on brief benchmarks. Software support and management capabilities, including Android Enterprise AI controls, also factor into device procurement.
Qualcomm maintains that the overheating reports are inaccurate, while Samsung’s processor decision remains unconfirmed. Independent testing of shipping devices will be the clearest measure of whether the alleged thermal concerns translate into real-world performance limitations.

Qualcomm sells Snapdragon processors through its QCT segment and licenses wireless patents through QTL. Its fiscal third quarter showed both sides of the business. AI Pivot Doubles Qualcomm's Non-Handset Target
Management raised its fiscal 2029 non-handset revenue target to $40 billion from $22 billion. That figure includes more than $15 billion in data center revenue. Two custom silicon projects with global-scale hyperscalers start producing revenue in the December quarter, and purchase orders are already in place. Non-handset growth is expected to speed up from 24% in FY2026 to above 60% in FY2027.
Automotive has posted 23 consecutive quarters of double-digit growth, and BMW has named Qualcomm its lead compute supplier. Even so, the stock trades at a forward P/E of about 20, with a PEG ratio of 0.88 and a free cash flow yield near 6.79%.

Custom-chip revenue will also lower QCT gross margin by 1.5% to 2%. Meanwhile, the core business keeps shrinking. Qualcomm's chips will appear in a much smaller share of new iPhones, and revenue from Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL) is expected to fall about 50% from the September quarter to the December quarter. Weakness in Android is expected to reduce EPS by more than $1.50.
Chief executive Cristiano Amon acknowledged the doubt directly: "investors want to see more proof points that we can successfully execute on our plans as a new entrant."
Price Increases and December Data Center Revenue Will Decide the Next Move
Qualcomm is raising prices by double-digit percentages to offset higher memory, wafer and packaging costs. Management expects QCT gross margin to return to 48% to 50% as those increases take effect. The current price already reflects a lot of handset weakness, but Qualcomm has not yet shown it can earn money in AI. Qualcomm Vs. Intel: The Market is Refuting Both AI Rebrand Attempts
Intel and Qualcomm both showed up to earnings with a fresh AI identity, but investors have been voting with their feet ever since. One company is already cashing AI checks while the other is asking you to fund a roadmap…
Published October 14, 2026, 10:45am ET · 3 min read
This image visualizes the intricate connection between artificial intelligence, robotics, and market performance, reflecting the ongoing debate about Tesla's evolution into a leading AI firm. © Summit Art Creations / Shutterstock.com
Intel (NASDAQ:INTC | INTC Price Prediction) and Qualcomm (NASDAQ:QCOM) each used their summer earnings reports to sell investors on an AI identity. Intel highlighted server CPUs, advanced packaging and foundry capacity. Qualcomm highlighted cars, custom silicon and a data center plan that has not yet booked its first revenue. Since those reports, investors have cooled on both stories.
Intel closed at $102.81, just under the $103.79 it traded at when it reported. It also fell 8.61% this week. After a 178.62% year-to-date run, the pivot looks priced in. Qualcomm is up only 5.03% this year, which is a weak verdict.
Xeon Lifts Intel While Phones Sink Qualcomm
Intel’s revenue rose 25.4% to $16.13 billion, its strongest growth in more than 15 years. Data Center and AI led the way, jumping 59% on Xeon demand from hyperscale and enterprise customers. CEO Lip-Bu Tan said “strong demand for our products continues to outpace our growing supply.” CFO David Zinsner called the client gains “largely ASP,” meaning price increases and product mix did the lifting.
Qualcomm’s revenue slipped 4.0% to $9.95 billion. Handsets fell 20% as memory inflation hit phone makers. Its share of upcoming iPhones will also land well below its earlier 20% estimate. Automotive climbed 61% to a record $1.59 billion. EPS of $2.21 just missed the $2.22 estimate, ending a six-quarter streak of beats.
Android and Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL) handsets
Intel’s AI case rests on products it already ships: x86 CPUs, EMIB-T packaging with a “growing EMIB-T backlog,” and 18A plants. Capital spending for 2026 now tops $20 billion. Foundry is the soft spot. It lost $2.1 billion on just $293 million of external revenue.
Qualcomm is asking investors to pay for a future. Management raised its fiscal 2029 non-handset target to $40 billion, including $15 billion from data center. Custom chips for two hyperscalers start producing revenue in the December quarter, and a September collaboration with Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) adds weight. However, those chips will initially cut QCT gross margin by 1.5% to 2%. CEO Cristiano Amon admitted that “investors want to see more proof points.”
Silicon Proof Will Decide Who Breaks Out
I am watching whether Intel’s 14A PDK 0.9, due in October, wins signed external foundry customers. For Qualcomm, keep an eye on its HBC silicon demonstration ahead of a mid-2027 launch. Also watch whether its double-digit price increases restore the historical 48% to 50% gross margin range.
Why I Lean Toward Intel’s Tangible AI Revenue
To me, Intel has the stronger AI evidence right now. AI-driven businesses generated roughly 70% of revenue, and the main constraint is supply. Still, the stock’s big run leaves little room if foundry struggles. Qualcomm’s case relies on automotive and a dividend raised to $0.92 to carry the business while data center grows. I would warm to Qualcomm once HBC performs on real silicon. Until then, Intel’s execution looks more solid to me (we reverse-engineered what the biggest AI chip winners looked like early and put the pattern in a free guide here: The Next Nvidia Playbook).

Qualcomm Technologies, Inc. announced its agreement to acquire PickNik Inc., an industry recognized robotics software company and longtime steward of MoveIt, one of the world's most widely adopted open-source robotics manipulation frameworks.
This acquisition is intended to strengthen Qualcomm Technologies' commitment to fostering an open robotics ecosystem, providing developers with the tools, software, and frameworks needed to move more efficiently from research and experimentation to prototyping, deployment, and production at scale.
In addition to remaining open-source, MoveIt is expected to offer streamlined integration with Dragonwing robotics platforms—providing developers with a more streamlined path from AI models such as VLAs and VLMs to planning, manipulation, and real-time control. The closing of this transaction is subject to customary closing conditions.
“Robotics is one of the most exciting frontiers of physical AI, and software is the connective tissue that turns great hardware into great robots,” said Nakul Duggal, EVP and Group GM, Automotive, Industrial and Embedded IoT, and Robotics, Qualcomm Technologies, Inc. “PickNik has earned tremendous trust within the global robotics community through its stewardship of MoveIt and its commitment to open-source innovation. Together, we plan to make it easier for developers to build advanced robotic applications on Dragonwing robotics platforms, while continuing to support the openness and collaboration that have made MoveIt successful.”
“Since our founding, PickNik’s mission has been to provide industries with a powerful, open platform that accelerates innovation and development of advanced robotics, well beyond traditional factories," said Dave Coleman, Founder and Chief Product Officer, PickNik Inc. “Joining Qualcomm Technologies will allow us to accelerate that mission, expand investment in MoveIt as a leading AI training platform for robotics, and deliver even more value to developers while preserving the openness, community collaboration, and cross-platform support that have always been central to our approach.”
“MoveIt is entering an exciting new chapter with the resources and support to help expand its impact,” said Dave Grant, Chief Executive Officer, PickNik Inc. “We look forward to joining Qualcomm Technologies and building on MoveIt’s momentum.”
Built atop the Robot Operating System (ROS), MoveIt has been used extensively by developers, students, researchers, and commercial robotics organizations worldwide to create sophisticated robotic applications in nearly every industry, including industrial automation, service robotics, mobile manipulation, and emerging physical AI systems.
Qualcomm Technologies and PickNik recognize that MoveIt’s value comes from its openness, broad adoption, and active developer community. Accordingly, Qualcomm Technologies intends for MoveIt to remain open-source under its existing license with community-driven roadmaps and open resources. Qualcomm Technologies also intends to continue supporting MoveIt across third-party hardware providers. MoveIt’s hardware-agnostic design is a key enabler of innovation, giving developers the freedom to choose the robot, compute platforms, and sensor components that best fit their needs.
Qualcomm Technologies and PickNik are both founding members of the Open Source Robotics Alliance (OSRA) and Qualcomm Technologies intends to continue driving major projects including Space ROS, a hardened version of ROS optimized for critical applications such as space exploration. Qualcomm Technologies will continue to support the open source development of MoveIt and ROS.
Accelerating Robotics Development on Dragonwing and Arduino
As part of the acquisition, MoveIt, MoveIt Pro — PickNik’s commercial platform designed to support advanced robotics systems — and future PickNik technologies, are poised to become more closely integrated with Dragonwing robotics platforms. This integration will enable developers to more easily take advantage of Dragonwing’s advanced AI, heterogeneous computing, connectivity, and real-time robotics capabilities in order to help simplify robotics development, shorten deployment timelines, and accelerate innovation across a broad range of robotic applications.
Developers building on Dragonwing should benefit from first-class, optimized support for MoveIt’s motion planning, manipulation, perception, and kinematics capabilities—helping to move from prototype to production faster while maintaining the flexibility to develop for diverse robotics architectures and deployment environments.
Starting with Arduino VENTUNO Q boards, MoveIt integration with Arduino aims to make advanced robotics, edge AI, and heterogeneous compute more accessible than ever. This integration seeks to extend powerful motion planning and autonomy capabilities to target millions of developers, helping shorten the journey from prototype to production-ready robots.
Qualcomm Technologies and PickNik displayed MoveIt Pro running on VENTUNO Q and Dragonwing robotics platforms last month at ROSCon Toronto.

pages.title: Qualcomm Wins Lawsuit Against Arm But Will Only Receive Two Bucks
pages.text:
Qualcomm wins lawsuit against Arm but will only receive two bucks
Arm accuses Qualcomm of filing the lawsuit to get out of paying ‘billions of dollars’ in royalties
Add Engadget on Google:
Both Arm and Qualcomm have published statements, saying that they were pleased with the findings of a Delaware jury in a breach of licensing lawsuit. That's because while the jury found that Arm breached its Architectural License Agreement with Qualcomm and acted to disrupt its business, it also only awarded the latter company a total of $2 in damages. Yes, just $2 — that figure isn't missing a million or a billion.
The two companies have been embroiled in legal battles for years. In 2022, Arm sued Qualcomm after the latter purchased Nuvia, which also licenses its technologies. Arm had argued at the time that Qualcomm didn't obtain the necessary permits to transfer Nuvia's licenses, constituting a breach of contract. Last year, Qualcomm announced that the court had granted it "complete victory" after it dismissed Arm's remaining claims.
According to Thurrott, due to the information that emerged during that case's discovery and the things Arm Holdings CEO Rene Haas' said on the stand, Qualcomm sued Arm. Reuters says that after a five-day trial, the jury found that Arm had breached their agreements by withholding software patches and tools for its designs. It also found that Arm intentionally interfered with Qualcomm's business deal with Meta. Qualcomm alleged that in 2024, Arm had leaked to Bloomberg News that it had breached a licensing agreement when it was on the verge of closing a deal with Meta, leading to a delay. The jury sided with Arm in four of Qualcomm's other claims.
In its statement, Arm said the lawsuit was an attempt by Qualcomm to get out of paying it "billions of dollars" under the companies' existing licensing agreements.
"We are pleased with the jury' decision today finding for Arm on four claims and awarding only one dollar in damages on each of Qualcomm's other two claims," Arm said. "Despite Qualcomm's pursuit of this case in an attempt to deprive Arm of billions of dollars under our license agreements, the jury's verdict confirms that Arm operated in good faith under its technology license agreement and its award of only two dollars confirms the merit of Arm's arguments in the case."
Meanwhile, Qualcomm said it was "gratified that the jury found Arm breached its long-standing Architectural License Agreement (ALA) with Qualcomm, failed to honor its commitments, and intentionally acted to disrupt Qualcomm's businesses." It added: "Together with Qualcomm's prior court victory, this outcome further exposes Arm's broader intentions to harm Qualcomm and its ecosystem."
Their court battle, however, is far from over. US District Judge ​Maryellen Noreika is still expected to resolve several more disputes between the companies. If Noreika ultimately sides with Qualcomm, the company could stop paying Arm royalties for five years, which as Arm said was worth billions of dollars. Arm argued that the penalty, as indicated in the companies' licensing contract, isn't enforceable.

Qualcomm is on track to bring its initial Wi-Fi 8 products to market towards the end of 2026, with the rollout expected to expand thereafter, according to a senior company executive.
Gautam Sheoran, Senior Vice President and General Manager, Connectivity, Broadband & Networking, Qualcomm told FE that the company is working with major OEM partners, including several existing Wi-Fi 7 partners, on the transition to Wi-Fi 8.

“Wi-Fi 8 is going to start at the end of this year with the most aggressive device makers, and then it’s going to expand in the next year,” he said.
The technology is designed to improve network reliability, increase capacity and reduce latency, particularly as connected devices increasingly support simultaneous applications such as gaming, video streaming, remote work and Internet of Things (IoT) services.
Qualcomm is additionally integrating artificial intelligence engines into network gateways to classify applications and traffic, allowing networks to prioritise bandwidth and maintain quality of service for latency-sensitive applications. The company is also working on network anomaly detection, troubleshooting and security applications.
“Every house has a gateway that provides you internet access. And that’s typically been a black box or a white box, getting data in, sending data out, not a lot of intelligence,” Sheoran said, adding that this is an area where the company expects rapid change.
The shift towards intelligent gateways is particularly relevant as consumers use multiple connected devices simultaneously, mainly for cloud gaming, where delays in network response can affect the user experience.

Sheoran added that for the first time, Qualcomm is putting a 4×4 Wi-Fi radio in its handset chips. It is also launching what it calls the industry’s first 5×5 radio for access points. The extra antennas extend range and improve stability. The chips integrate AI engines that prioritise traffic, so that gaming, work calls and streaming do not compete in busy homes. The company has also worked on cutting power consumption, he added.
On top of this sits Qualcomm’s Dragonwing Network AI suite, which classifies traffic, applications and devices, Sheoran said that the firm seeks to develop in-home sensing and security features. “Edge security, especially in the gateways, is going to become more and more important,” Sheoran said, adding that hacking is getting easier.
India is major base for Qualcomm’s chip and software development, Sheoran said, calling the talent base and the volume of work as extremely integral.

Can Qualcomm's PickNik Acquisition Strengthen Its Robotics Edge?
Tue, October 20, 2026 at 8:09 AM CDT 2 min read
Qualcomm Incorporated QCOM is strengthening its position in the rapidly evolving robotics market through its proposed acquisition of PickNik Robotics, a developer of advanced robotics software. The transaction aligns with Qualcomm's strategy to expand its footprint in physical artificial intelligence (AI), edge computing and intelligent robotics.
PickNik is recognized for its stewardship of MoveIt, a widely adopted open-source robotics manipulation framework built on the Robot Operating System (ROS). The platform supports motion planning, manipulation and robotic control across industrial automation, service robotics and emerging physical AI applications. The transaction, subject to customary closing conditions, could strengthen Qualcomm's ability to offer integrated hardware and software solutions.
The buyout is expected to enhance Qualcomm's Dragonwing Robotics platforms by integrating MoveIt and PickNik's commercial MoveIt Pro software. This combination could enable developers to leverage Qualcomm's AI processing, connectivity and heterogeneous computing capabilities alongside advanced motion planning and real-time robotic control.
The integration is also expected to extend to Arduino platforms, beginning with VENTUNO Q boards. This could make advanced robotics development more accessible to a broader developer community while accelerating the transition from prototypes to commercial deployments.
Importantly, Qualcomm intends to maintain MoveIt as an open-source framework supporting third-party hardware. This approach could encourage wider ecosystem participation and strengthen developer engagement, potentially boosting adoption of its Dragonwing platforms.
Physical AI Opportunities Support Long-Term Diversification
The planned acquisition complements Qualcomm's broader efforts to diversify beyond smartphones into automotive, industrial IoT and edge AI markets. Its March 2026 collaboration with NEURA Robotics to advance cognitive robotics and humanoid applications further underscores its growing focus on physical AI.
Combining PickNik's software expertise with Qualcomm's power-efficient computing capabilities could improve its competitive positioning as demand for intelligent automation increases across industrial and commercial applications.
However, the acquisition's financial terms remain undisclosed, limiting visibility into its immediate earnings contribution. Integration challenges, competition in robotics computing and uncertain commercialization timelines could also constrain near-term benefits. Stiff competition from NVIDIA Corporation NVDA, Broadcom Inc. AVGO and Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. AMD further strains its margins.
Nevertheless, PickNik's established developer ecosystem and robotics software capabilities could help Qualcomm expand its addressable market and deepen customer engagement. Successful integration may strengthen QCOM's position in next-generation robotics while supporting its long-term diversification strategy.

Qualcomm is rejecting overheating allegations involving its most powerful new smartphone processor, as questions grow over whether Samsung will use the chip in its Galaxy S27 Ultra.
On October 17, Qualcomm rejected reports of thermal problems with the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6. The response followed South Korean reporting that Samsung had encountered performance slowdowns while testing the processor and was considering its Exynos 2700 chip as an alternative.
Samsung has not confirmed the alleged findings or announced a processor change. The dispute leaves questions about how Qualcomm’s new flagship chip will perform under sustained workloads in finished phones.
Qualcomm disputes Samsung testing allegations
The allegations originated in an October 16 Seoul Economic Daily report, which cited industry sources claiming Samsung’s internal tests found excessive temperatures and repeated performance slowdowns during demanding workloads.
Samsung reportedly requested improvements from Qualcomm and was weighing the Exynos 2700 if the Snapdragon processor failed to meet its requirements. Subsequent reporting indicated discussions could continue through the end of October.
Qualcomm rejected the allegations in a statement to 9to5Google, describing reports of thermal problems involving the Extreme chip as “inaccurate.”
Chief Marketing Officer Don McGuire separately wrote on X that there were “no systemic thermal issues” with the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6. He added that manufacturers routinely adjust performance and power consumption during device development.
McGuire did not explicitly identify the Extreme variant in his remarks, an ambiguity highlighted by Android Authority on October 19. Qualcomm’s separate statement addressed that processor directly, but neither company has publicly released data establishing whether the alleged problems occurred.
Qualcomm’s official specifications list a 2-nanometer manufacturing process and CPU speeds reaching 5GHz. Those figures describe the processor’s capabilities, not how consistently finished devices can maintain peak performance.
Qualcomm also introduced a standard Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6, with its features detailed in a separate platform overview. Samsung has not announced plans to replace Snapdragon in its Galaxy S27 Ultra.
Thermal throttling reduces processor speeds as temperatures rise. Although normal in modern chips, excessive throttling can disrupt demanding workloads, including gaming, prolonged video recording and on-device AI processing.
Peak benchmark scores cannot establish sustained performance on their own. Cooling hardware, battery capacity and software tuning also influence how individual smartphones manage heat.
Motorola’s upcoming Signature 27 flagship will feature the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 and an ArcticMesh cooling system designed to sustain performance under load. Whether that design delivers consistent results will require independent testing.
Organizations evaluating Snapdragon-powered phones should compare performance, battery behavior and temperatures during repeated workloads rather than relying on brief benchmarks. Software support and management capabilities, including Android Enterprise AI controls, also factor into device procurement.
Qualcomm maintains that the overheating reports are inaccurate, while Samsung’s processor decision remains unconfirmed. Independent testing of shipping devices will be the clearest measure of whether the alleged thermal concerns translate into real-world performance limitations.

Through its planned acquisition of PickNik, Qualcomm Technologies aims to strengthen its robotics software portfolio and accelerate development on its Dragonwing platforms.
Qualcomm Technologies, Inc. announced its agreement to acquire PickNik Inc., an industry recognized robotics software company and longtime steward of MoveIt, one of the world's most widely adopted open-source robotics manipulation frameworks.
This acquisition is intended to strengthen Qualcomm Technologies' commitment to fostering an open robotics ecosystem, providing developers with the tools, software, and frameworks needed to move more efficiently from research and experimentation to prototyping, deployment, and production at scale.
In addition to remaining open-source, MoveIt is expected to offer streamlined integration with Dragonwing robotics platforms—providing developers with a more streamlined path from AI models such as VLAs and VLMs to planning, manipulation, and real-time control. The closing of this transaction is subject to customary closing conditions.
“Robotics is one of the most exciting frontiers of physical AI, and software is the connective tissue that turns great hardware into great robots,” said Nakul Duggal, EVP and Group GM, Automotive, Industrial and Embedded IoT, and Robotics, Qualcomm Technologies, Inc. “PickNik has earned tremendous trust within the global robotics community through its stewardship of MoveIt and its commitment to open-source innovation. Together, we plan to make it easier for developers to build advanced robotic applications on Dragonwing robotics platforms, while continuing to support the openness and collaboration that have made MoveIt successful.”
“Since our founding, PickNik’s mission has been to provide industries with a powerful, open platform that accelerates innovation and development of advanced robotics, well beyond traditional factories," said Dave Coleman, Founder and Chief Product Officer, PickNik Inc. “Joining Qualcomm Technologies will allow us to accelerate that mission, expand investment in MoveIt as a leading AI training platform for robotics, and deliver even more value to developers while preserving the openness, community collaboration, and cross-platform support that have always been central to our approach.”
“MoveIt is entering an exciting new chapter with the resources and support to help expand its impact,” said Dave Grant, Chief Executive Officer, PickNik Inc. “We look forward to joining Qualcomm Technologies and building on MoveIt’s momentum.”
Built atop the Robot Operating System (ROS), MoveIt has been used extensively by developers, students, researchers, and commercial robotics organizations worldwide to create sophisticated robotic applications in nearly every industry, including industrial automation, service robotics, mobile manipulation, and emerging physical AI systems.
Qualcomm Technologies and PickNik recognize that MoveIt’s value comes from its openness, broad adoption, and active developer community. Accordingly, Qualcomm Technologies intends for MoveIt to remain open-source under its existing license with community-driven roadmaps and open resources. Qualcomm Technologies also intends to continue supporting MoveIt across third-party hardware providers. MoveIt’s hardware-agnostic design is a key enabler of innovation, giving developers the freedom to choose the robot, compute platforms, and sensor components that best fit their needs.
Qualcomm Technologies and PickNik are both founding members of the Open Source Robotics Alliance (OSRA) and Qualcomm Technologies intends to continue driving major projects including Space ROS, a hardened version of ROS optimized for critical applications such as space exploration. Qualcomm Technologies will continue to support the open source development of MoveIt and ROS.
Accelerating Robotics Development on Dragonwing and Arduino
As part of the acquisition, MoveIt, MoveIt Pro — PickNik’s commercial platform designed to support advanced robotics systems — and future PickNik technologies, are poised to become more closely integrated with Dragonwing robotics platforms. This integration will enable developers to more easily take advantage of Dragonwing’s advanced AI, heterogeneous computing, connectivity, and real-time robotics capabilities in order to help simplify robotics development, shorten deployment timelines, and accelerate innovation across a broad range of robotic applications.
Developers building on Dragonwing should benefit from first-class, optimized support for MoveIt’s motion planning, manipulation, perception, and kinematics capabilities—helping to move from prototype to production faster while maintaining the flexibility to develop for diverse robotics architectures and deployment environments.
Starting with Arduino VENTUNO Q boards, MoveIt integration with Arduino aims to make advanced robotics, edge AI, and heterogeneous compute more accessible than ever. This integration seeks to extend powerful motion planning and autonomy capabilities to target millions of developers, helping shorten the journey from prototype to production-ready robots.

Can Qualcomm's PickNik Acquisition Strengthen Its Robotics Edge?
Tue, October 20, 2026 at 8:09 AM CDT 2 min read
Qualcomm Incorporated QCOM is strengthening its position in the rapidly evolving robotics market through its proposed acquisition of PickNik Robotics, a developer of advanced robotics software. The transaction aligns with Qualcomm's strategy to expand its footprint in physical artificial intelligence (AI), edge computing and intelligent robotics.
PickNik is recognized for its stewardship of MoveIt, a widely adopted open-source robotics manipulation framework built on the Robot Operating System (ROS). The platform supports motion planning, manipulation and robotic control across industrial automation, service robotics and emerging physical AI applications. The transaction, subject to customary closing conditions, could strengthen Qualcomm's ability to offer integrated hardware and software solutions.
The buyout is expected to enhance Qualcomm's Dragonwing Robotics platforms by integrating MoveIt and PickNik's commercial MoveIt Pro software. This combination could enable developers to leverage Qualcomm's AI processing, connectivity and heterogeneous computing capabilities alongside advanced motion planning and real-time robotic control.
The integration is also expected to extend to Arduino platforms, beginning with VENTUNO Q boards. This could make advanced robotics development more accessible to a broader developer community while accelerating the transition from prototypes to commercial deployments.
Importantly, Qualcomm intends to maintain MoveIt as an open-source framework supporting third-party hardware. This approach could encourage wider ecosystem participation and strengthen developer engagement, potentially boosting adoption of its Dragonwing platforms.
Physical AI Opportunities Support Long-Term Diversification
The planned acquisition complements Qualcomm's broader efforts to diversify beyond smartphones into automotive, industrial IoT and edge AI markets. Its March 2026 collaboration with NEURA Robotics to advance cognitive robotics and humanoid applications further underscores its growing focus on physical AI.
Combining PickNik's software expertise with Qualcomm's power-efficient computing capabilities could improve its competitive positioning as demand for intelligent automation increases across industrial and commercial applications.
However, the acquisition's financial terms remain undisclosed, limiting visibility into its immediate earnings contribution. Integration challenges, competition in robotics computing and uncertain commercialization timelines could also constrain near-term benefits. Stiff competition from NVIDIA Corporation NVDA, Broadcom Inc. AVGO and Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. AMD further strains its margins.
Nevertheless, PickNik's established developer ecosystem and robotics software capabilities could help Qualcomm expand its addressable market and deepen customer engagement. Successful integration may strengthen QCOM's position in next-generation robotics while supporting its long-term diversification strategy.
